Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Specify the components of a quiet knee postinjury or preoperatively.
Assess the goals of each stage of the rehabilitation process and determine key milestones.
Apply considerations for graft type and meniscal status into rehabilitation recommendations.
Identify the critical components of evidence-based postoperative rehabilitation.
Identify key considerations for safe return to play after anterior cruciate ligament rupture.
Initial Phase After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tear or
Reconstruction
Patients should undergo progressive, preoperative rehabilitation before proceeding with
surgical versus nonsurgical treatment.1

Patients should undergo surgical treatment with a quiet knee, which includes little to no joint
effusion and pain, full active and passive range of motion, no obvious walking impairments,
and a quadriceps strength index greater or equal to 70%.
Quadriceps strength is essential in preoperative and postoperative rehabilitation, with
preoperative quadriceps strength predicting better postoperative outcomes.2,3
Crutches should be discontinued if a normalized gait pattern is observed by a rehabilitation
professional, with good active quadriceps control and no extension lag with the straight leg
raise test; effusion should be less than 2+.
Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) must be performed immediately after injury and
surgical management to combat quadriceps inhibition.4,5
Neuromuscular training with cushions, disks, and balance boards; perturbation training;
and/or commercially available devices should be used to progressively improve dynamic joint
stability.

Initial Phase After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tear or
Reconstruction
Preoperative rehabilitation leads to better patient-reported outcomes, function, and
return-to-sport rates if combined with appropriate time frames for healing and
progressive postoperative rehabilitation.6–8 Re-gaining extension range of motion equal
to that of the uninvolved side as soon as possible should be the priority during the first
week of management after an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear. Effusion can be
monitored via a stroke test, which is a reliable clinical test used to grade intracapsular
swelling in the knee joint.9 A quiet knee also is the immediate goal after ACL
reconstruction. After a quiet knee is achieved, preoperative rehabilitation should include
components of progressive strength training, agility exercises, plyometric training, and
neuromuscular re-education.10 Perturbation training, a neuromuscular training
program, is a 10-session series of balance and proprioceptive training that can be used
to progress ACL-deficient athletes back to sport after milestones are met.1,11 NMES must
not be confused with transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation for pain management.
NMES should induce aggressive involuntary quadriceps contractions to patient

tolerance. Rehabilitation providers should understand the difference in these modalities
because terms such as electrotherapy or e-stim may be interpreted both ways.
Rehabilitation Considerations After ACL Reconstruction
Patients should be progressed through rehabilitation with the consideration of multiple
factors, including response to treatment, graft type, meniscal status, and biologic healing
times.

Rehabilitation Considerations After ACL Reconstruction
Patellar tendon autografts (bone-patellar tendon-bone) may cause anterior knee pain,
which can be managed via noxious electrical stimulation as necessary. After bone-
patellar tendon-bone grafting, modifications of the strengthening program may be
considered as necessary (eg, forces on patellofemoral joint during resistive exercises).
Knee flexion angles most comfortable for patients during NMES management typically
are between 45° and 60°. Quadriceps tendon autografts are associated with similar
restrictions as bone-patellar tendon-bone autografts, with the addition of the hip-flexion
angle being less than or equal to 45° during knee extension exercises (open kinetic chain
and NMES) to focus on healing the rectus femoris graft source. After hamstring tendon
autografting, isometric knee flexion should be avoided until 6 weeks postoperatively or
later. Resisted dynamic knee flexion should begin no earlier than 8 weeks
postoperatively and should be pain-free between 0° and 90° from 8 to 12 weeks
postoperatively. Typically, restrictions are lifted after 12 weeks postoperatively.
Plyometrics should be delayed until 16 weeks postoperatively. Overall, patients with an
allograft should undergo a slower progression for running and plyometrics because of
slower graft incorporation. For simple meniscus repair, weight bearing as tolerated
should be considered throughout rehabilitation. The knee will be locked in full extension
or a knee immobilizer immediately postoperatively. Range of motion should be
progressed on a weekly basis. For more complex meniscus repair, range of motion
progression will be slower. Isolated hamstring strengthening should be avoided for 8 to

10 weeks postoperatively, with no squatting below 60° permitted for 8 weeks
postoperatively and no squatting with twisting permitted for 16 weeks postoperatively.
Structuring Rehabilitation After ACL Tear or ACL Reconstruction
Postoperative rehabilitation should be criterion-based and progressive to ensure patients are
ready to enter the return to sport phase of rehabilitation.12–14
Quadriceps strength should be measured objectively and tracked throughout rehabilitation.
Appropriate rehabilitation should include the combined use of open and closed kinetic chain
exercises.15–19
Rehabilitation exercises must be performed with an appropriate volume, intensity, and
frequency to provide the stimulus for strength improvement.

Structuring Rehabilitation After ACL Tear or ACL Reconstruction
Objective measurements of quadriceps strength throughout rehabilitation are the only
method to understand when patients have met criteria for rehabilitation progression or
discharge. Quadriceps strength should be measured via an electromechanical
dynamometer if possible.20 If an electromechanical dynamometer is not available, a one-
repetition maximum test on a knee extension machine is used.20 Closed kinetic chain
strength testing for the quadriceps is not appropriate because it overestimates strength
of the quadriceps and allows for compensation.20 For quadriceps strengthening, open
kinetic chain exercises must be performed to achieve appropriate quadriceps strength
gains. Immediate open kinetic chain exercises should not be avoided because of fear of
strain on the graft. While walking, the strain on the ACL is two to three times the strain of
open kinetic chain knee extension.19 No difference in ACL laxity exists between those
who perform open versus closed kinetic chain exercises after ACL reconstruction. Open
kinetic chain exercises with the use of a knee extension machine or an
electromechanical dynamometer are the only methods to isolate the quadriceps. NMES
should be performed to patient tolerance until at least 80% quadriceps strength
symmetry is achieved. Open kinetic chain exercises should be dosed to muscle failure
early in rehabilitation and should be at least 60% to 70% of the one-repetition maximum

4/15

as patients progress through rehabilitation.19 Exercises should be loaded progressively,
and pain should be maintained below a 5/10 on the visual analog scale.21 Soreness
rules22 and knee effusion grades9 should be used to guide progression and type of
exercises. Clinicians should consistently assess responses to exercises. If effusion
increases in response to an exercise, the patient should remain at the same intensity or
decrease intensity. Exercises should not be progressed in patients with a 2+ effusion
(Resource 1).
Postoperative Criterion-based Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation programs should be divided into three phases followed by a return to play
training phase.12
High-intensity NMES should be included.
High-intensity NMES can be discontinued if involved quadriceps muscle strength is at least
80% of that of the uninvolved side.

Postoperative Criterion-based Rehabilitation
Early postoperative rehabilitation should begin on postoperative day one but no later
than 1 week postoperatively and should focus on early activation of the quadriceps;
normalization of walking gait patterns; and restoration of full and symmetric knee range
of motion, especially extension. Middle-stage rehabilitation should focus on continuing
to aggressively load the quadriceps and other lower extremity musculature and
beginning to introduce basic balance and neuromuscular control/proprioceptive
exercises. Selection of exercise and management should depend on response to
treatment, graft type, healing times, and patient goals. Late-stage rehabilitation should
focus on continued quadriceps strengthening; functional activity progression; and
beginning to shift toward sport-specific training, such as the initiation of running
progression or perturbation training.
Return to Play

A battery of functional performance testing and patient-reported outcome measures should
be used to clear patients to return to sports activity.23–25
Not meeting criteria for return to sport activity and returning to level I sports activity before 9
months postoperatively are independent risk factors for re-injury of the ACL.26
Secondary prevention programs should be incorporated after athletes have been cleared for
return to sports activity before full return to play.
Current evidence does not support the concept that persistent strength deficits and abnormal
kinematics noted at the time of return to sports activity will normalize quickly via routine
sports activity and training.

Return to Play
Patients should begin running progression after they demonstrate full range of motion, a
quadriceps strength index greater or equal to 80%, trace or less effusion, and minimal to
no joint pain or soreness. Agility exercises and multidirectional training generally begin
approximately 12 weeks postinjury or postoperatively.
Best evidence recommends waiting until at least 9 months postoperatively to return to
sports activity, with data suggesting that the re-injury rate is reduced by approximately
50% for each month return to sports activity is delayed until 9 months postoperatively.
Additional evidence shows similar risk reduction persists until 12 months
postoperatively.26–28
The return-to-sport decision should be based on various considerations. Ideally, all
patients should wait at least 9 months postoperatively per best evidence, with
consideration of biologic healing times. Rehabilitation status, assessed via functional
performance, is extremely important. Patients must meet stringent return-to-sport
criteria and have adequate training to return to their pre-injury level of activity. Patient
goals are important to consider in deciding the timing of return to sports activity (and in
selecting surgical versus nonsurgical management). Is this the last season of a patient’s
career and they must play? Does the patient have a long future career, in which case
losing 3 months of play time may be worth the inconvenience given the risks of re-injury?
A patient’s psychological readiness to return to sport also is important to consider.

Single-leg hop tests (single hop for distance, crossover hop for distance, triple hop for
distance, 6-meter timed hop) should be within 90% of the limb symmetry index
compared with the uninvolved leg (Figure 1). Quadriceps strength, assessed via maximal
voluntary isometric contraction with the use of an isometric or isokinetic dynamometer,
if possible (one-repetition maximum test on a knee extension machine is the best
alternative), should be at least 90% of that of the uninvolved limb (Figure 2). Patients
should score at least 90% on the Global Rating Scale of Perceived Function and the Knee
Outcome Survey Activities of Daily Living Scale. Secondary prevention programs should
include a multimodal approach (eg, strengthening, agility, plyometrics) and be
performed multiple times per week for at least 30 minutes.10,29 Biomechanical
screening can detect abnormal kinematics (transverse plane hip kinetics and frontal
plane knee kinematics during landing, sagittal plane knee moments at landing, and
deficits in postural stability) which have been shown to be independent predictors of
recurrent ACL injury.30–32

Psychological Readiness to Return to Sports Activity
Emerging evidence has suggested an optimal range of psychological readiness to return to
sports activity exists.33-36
Caution should be exercised in interpreting the results of psychological outcomes because
high psychological readiness may not necessarily indicate the athlete is safe to return to sports
activity and may lead to premature return to sports activity.

Psychological Readiness to Return to Sports Activity
Athletes who score higher on psychological readiness measures are more likely to return
to the same level of play or higher; however, greater knee-related confidence at a
younger age also may be related to higher re-injury rates. The ACL Return to Sport after
Injury Scale is a valid and reliable questionnaire that targets psychological readiness and
should be used during rehabilitation.36,37
Summary
Early achievement of a quiet knee (full and symmetric range of motion, trace or less effusion)
Early restoration of gait symmetry
Early and aggressive open kinetic chain quadriceps strengthening (open kinetic chain knee
extension is safe if dosed appropriately) and NMES to tolerance (not the same as
transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation)
Use of objective measures (quadriceps strength testing, outcome measures, hop testing, etc.)
for progression and return-to-sport decision making

Guidelines for running progression, return-to-sport training initiation, perturbation training
Delaying return to sport as late as possible (at least 9 months postoperatively) to reduce risks
of re-injury while considering personal factors (eg, an athlete trying to return for the last
season of his or her career versus an athlete with a long future career); this conversation
should happen with the athlete/parents at an early stage to set expectations.
